title.text: Seeing and stopping in bad weather

narration.text: This lesson covers driving when visibility drops or the road is wet. Smoke, fog and downpours call for real headlights on low beam, wipers, defrosted glass and painted-line guides, along with fewer cabin distractions and attention to slow or parked rigs. Rain brings its own dangers: wipers mean headlights, fresh rain slicks the pavement, and stops get longer. Hydroplaning, wet brakes and flooded roads each have a rule of their own. In short: Smoke, fog, and downpours demand real headlights on low beams, lights with wipers, defrosted glass, and painted-line guides.

In smoke, fog or downpours, use your real headlights on low beam, never parking lamps alone. Run the wipers, keep the glass defrosted and use the painted lines as your guide. Murky driving also means cutting cabin distractions, watching for rigs that are crawling or parked, and keeping the glass and lamps clean. In a worked example, a driver meets heavy fog on a highway, turns on low-beam headlights and wipers, defrosts the glass and follows the painted lines. In short: Smoke, fog, and downpours demand real headlights on low beams, lights with wipers, defrosted glass, and painted-line guides.

narration.text: When your wipers are on, your headlights must be on too. Fresh rain slicks oiled pavement, which makes stops longer, so your following gap must grow. Hydroplaning happens when tires float off the road surface and into a skid. Soft tire pressure, bald tread and speed all make it worse. So the rules for rain are to light up, add space, and keep your tires and your speed in a condition that does not invite floating. In short: Wipers summon headlights, fresh rains slick oiled pavement into longer stops, and gaps grow accordingly. So when you reach water covering the road, the answer is to turn around, and after driving through deep puddles, test and dry the brakes gently.
